title: Using Interleaved Practice to Foster Spelling Acquisition https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0959475225000702
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), May 28, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises Klimovich and Richter's preregistered classroom experiment with 108 German third-graders, the first study to test interleaved practice specifically for spelling acquisition. Children who practised easily-confused spelling rules, like 'i' versus 'ie', in an interleaved sequence made fewer errors than those in blocked practice, both immediately and at an eight-week follow-up, and the interleaving benefit extended to new, untrained words that followed the same rules, suggesting genuine rule generalisation rather than rote memorisation. Barton highlights the classic desirable-difficulty signature here too: children found interleaved practice harder, predicted lower success, and made more errors during practice itself, even though it produced better long-term outcomes. Crucially, the long-term benefit was concentrated in children with average-to-high prior knowledge; children with low prior knowledge didn't show the same gain, suggesting interleaving may need extra scaffolding, or simply more practice time, for weaker spellers.
points: Interleaved practice on easily-confused spelling rules cut errors both immediately after training and at an eight-week follow-up, versus blocked practice.
The interleaving benefit generalised to new, untrained words following the same spelling rules — evidence that children were learning the underlying rule, not just memorising specific words.
Interleaving only produced significant long-term benefits for children with average-to-high prior knowledge; children with low prior knowledge did not show the same gain.

The classic desirable-difficulty pattern held: children rated interleaved practice as harder, predicted lower success, and made more errors during practice, despite it producing better long-term learning.
Barton flags that interleaving works best specifically for highly similar, easily-confused rules — simply mixing unrelated spelling topics isn't expected to help.
quotes: The study found that interleaved practice led to fewer spelling errors immediately after training and in a follow-up test eight weeks later, especially benefiting children with average to high prior knowledge.

While interleaved practice was perceived as more difficult and resulted in more errors during the practice phase, these characteristics align with the concept of desirable difficulties which promote long-term retention.
This interleaving benefit persisted after an 8-week follow-up for the trained and new words for children with average to high prior knowledge of word spellings
Children with low prior knowledge did not show a significant benefit from interleaved practice in the follow-up test.
Children perceived interleaving as less effective than blocked practice, even though it led to better long-term outcomes for many.
The authors suggest that interleaving can be a valuable instructional method for literacy acquisition when applied to highly similar concepts.
